title: Holding Regulators to Account
summary: Why regulators are given independence, the accountability mechanisms parliament controls, and how to conduct effective scrutiny hearings and inquiries.
contentGaps: Written as part of a programme: Aim and Purpose is the module's one-line description; audience, prior knowledge and core reading come from the programme

sections.Aim and Purpose: Why regulators are given independence, the accountability mechanisms parliament controls, and how to conduct effective scrutiny hearings and inquiries.
Learning Objectives: Explain the rationale for regulatory independence and its limits
Use annual reports, hearings and inquiries to scrutinise regulators
Distinguish legitimate scrutiny from interference in individual cases
Syllabus: Annual reports, budgets and performance information
Preparing for and conducting a scrutiny hearing
A question set for regulators and ministers
Intended Audience: Members of parliament, particularly those on finance, economic affairs, budget and public accounts committees
Committee clerks, researchers and parliamentary library staff supporting financial scrutiny
Advisers to parliamentarians and party policy staff working on financial issues
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: No prior knowledge of financial services or regulation is required. Experience of committee work is helpful.
Core Reading: OECD (2014), The Governance of Regulators, OECD Best Practice Principles for Regulatory Policy
G20/OECD (2022), High-Level Principles on Financial Consumer Protection
FATF (2012, updated), International Standards on Combating Money Laundering and the Financing of Terrorism and Proliferation: The FATF Recommendations
IOSCO (2017), Objectives and Principles of Securities Regulation
